1. The present is a complaint filed under section 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (PFA Act), alleging that the accused persons have violated the provisions of the PFA Act and Rules.
The accused no.1 is stated to be the vendor of M/s. Arora Traders, from where the food article, that is, 'Mustard Oil' was lifted for sampling.
Accused no.2 (since expired) was the Proprietor of M/s.

sentences.text: Accused no.3 Company is stated to be the manufacturer / supplier from whom the vendor had purchased the food article and accused no.4 is stated to be its Nominee.

2. As per the complaint, on 13.09.2000, the food officials consisting of Food Inspector (FI)
Dharmavir Singh and FI A. K. Gupta under the supervision of Local Health Authority (LHA)/SDM Sh. G. R. Meena reached along with their staff at the premises of M/s. Arora Traders at H-12,
Shradhanand Market, Delhi-06, where the accused no.1 was found conducting the business of various food articles, which were lying stored/exposed for sale for human consumption.

The FI disclosed his identity and expressed his intention to purchase a sample of 'Mustard Oil' from the vendor that was lying in sealed bottles of 455 gram each bearing identical label declaration, to which he agreed.
The sample was then lifted as per procedure prescribed under the PFA Act and Rules.
Each sample was separately packed, fastened, marked and sealed and necessary documents were prepared at the spot, including the Notice as per Form-VI, panchnama etc.
The price of sample was paid to the vendor.
Thereafter, one counterpart of the sample was sent to the Public Analyst (PA) in intact condition and the other two counterparts were deposited with SDM/LHA.

Vide report dated 29.09.2000, the PA found the sample to be not conforming to standards on the ground that its saponification and iodine values exceeded the prescribed maximum limits, and also that the sample was misbranded being in violation of Rule 32(c) of PFA Rules.
Upon receipt of report, the SDM/LHA ordered investigation which was carried out by FI.
It was found that accused no.2 was the proprietor of the vendor business concern and that the sample had been purchased by them from accused no.3 company, of which accused no.4 was the nominee.
After completion of investigation, sanction under section 20 of the PFA Act was obtained from the Director PFA.

The complaint was then filed in the court on 06.09.2001 alleging violation of section 2(ia)(a), (b) and (m) of PFA Act, and also section 2(ix)(k) of PFA Act read with rule 32(c) of PFA Rules, as punishable section 7/16(1)(a) of PFA Act.
3. As the complaint was filed in writing by a public servant, recording of pre-summoning evidence was dispensed with and the accused persons were summoned.

The accused appeared and filed an application under section 13(2) of PFA Act thereby exercising the right to get the second counterpart of the sample to be analysed from Central Food Laboratory (CFL).
The application was allowed and a counterpart was sent for analysis to CFL.
The CFL examined the sample and its Director gave Certificate dated 11.02.2002, opining the sample to be misbranded being in violation of section 2(ix)(g) of PFA Act.

4. Though the offence was only of misbranding and was summons triable in nature, it was listed for pre charge evidence vide order dated 23.11.2005 (a pro secure prescribed for warrants triable complaint case).
Pre charge evidence was led wherein PW1 FI D. V. Singh was examined by the prosecution.

Based on his testimony, charge was framed against accused no.1 and 3 (by that time,
accused no.2 had already expired and accused no.4 had been declared proclaimed offender) on 23.03.2009 for commission of the offence punishable under section 7/16(1)(a) PFA Act, being violation of section 2(ix)(g) of PFA Act, to which they pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.
The said charge was subsequently amended on 04.03.2016 to remove a formal technical difficulty.

sentences.text: At the trial, prosecution examined three witness in support of its case.
PW-1 FI D. V. Singh, PW-2 FI Arun Kumar Gupta and PW-3 Sh. G. R. Meena were a part of the team that had visited the spot for sample proceedings.

They deposed about the proceedings conducted by them on 13.09.2000 and narrated the steps undertaken by them during the sample proceedings, including disclosing their identity, expressing intention to purchase sample for analysis, lifting the sample of 3 sealed bottles of 455 gram each of 'Mustard Oil, separately sealing, marking the sample bottles, and obtaining signatures of vendor and witnesses.

They also proved the necessary documents including the vendor's receipt Ex. PW-1/A, notice Ex. PW-1/B, panchnama Ex. PW-1/C, notice under section 14A Ex. PW1/D, PA Receipt Ex. PW-1/E and LHA receipt Ex. PW-1/F. PA report Ex. PW-1/G was received and investigation was started.
Letters
Ex . PW- 1/H to Ex. PW1/R10
were written and replies taken during the course of investigation.

After completion of investigation, sanction Ex.
PW-1/S was taken from the Director PFA.
The complaint Ex. PW-1/T was filed in the court.
A copy of PA report with intimation letter Ex. PW-1/U was sent to the accused persons vide postal receipt Ex. PW-1/V.

These witnesses were duly cross-examined by Ld. Defence Counsel wherein they denied that the sampling method was not proper or that the accused persons had been falsely implicated.
6.
Statements of the accused no.1 and AR of accused no.3 under section 313 CrPC were recorded on 13.08.2014 wherein they denied the allegations and pleaded innocence.
Though PW-1 admitted the sample proceedings, yet he claimed that a representative sample was not taken.
He took stand that he had purchased the article from accused no.3 against a proper bill.
Accused no.3 denied the knowledge about the sample proceedings but claimed that the reports of analysts were not reliable being at variation and it claimed that all the rules had been complied with.
The accused persons did not lead any evidence in defence.

7. It is in these circumstances, Ld. SPP for the complainant has argued that the complainant has been able to establish its case against both the accused no.1 and 3 beyond reasonable doubt, on the ground that the accused persons have not been able to rebut the findings in the CFL report dated 11.02.2002 which as per section 13(3) of PFA Act is final and conclusive.
It is submitted that all the witnesses have supported its case and no contradiction can be seen in their testimony.
8. On the other hand, respective Ld. Defence Counsel have submitted that the sample proceedings were not conducted properly and that there are various missing links in the testimony of the witnesses.

Ld. Counsel have strongly contended that there is variation in the reports as given by PA and CFL, which leads to conclusion that the two samples were not representative and therefore,
conviction cannot be based solely on the basis of the CFL report.
They have relied upon the various judgements in their support.
9. I have heard the arguments advanced by Ld. SPP for the complainant and respective Ld. Defence Counsel for the accused persons and have carefully perused the material available on record.

10. It is to be understood that the charge / notice framed against the accused persons is for violation of section 2(ix)(g) of the PFA Act on the basis of CFL report, that pertains to the offence of misbranding only.
Under section 2(ix)(g) of PFA Act, a package or the label on the package should Delhi Administration / Food Inspector vs A-1.

11. In the case at hand, it is an admitted position, as is clear from both the reports of PA and CFL that the food article Mustard Oil is a part of Appendix-B of the PFA Rules and is a standardized food article.
12. As per section 13(3) of the PFA Act, the certificate issued by the Director of CFL shall supersede the report of the PA.
As per proviso to section 13(5) of the Act, such certificate shall be final and conclusive evidence for the facts stated therein.
Thus, as far as the findings of the CFL are concerned, the same are final and conclusive and no evidence can be given to disprove the same.

13. In Calcutta Municipal Corporation v. Pawan Kumar Saraf [AIR 1999 SC 738], it has been authoritatively laid down that the legal impact of a certificate of the Director of CFL is three fold: (a)
it annuls or replaces the report of the PA, (b) it gains finality regarding the quality and standard of the food article involved in the case and (c) it becomes irrefutable so far as the facts stated therein are concerned.
14.

entities.text: Calcutta Municipal Corporation v. Pawan Kumar Saraf [AIR 1999 SC 738]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In Subhash Chander v. State, Delhi Administration [1983(4) DRJ 100], it was observed by Hon'ble High Court of Delhi that "It has repeatedly been held by the supreme court that the certificate of the Director supersedes the report of the public analyst and is to be treated as conclusive evidence of its contents.

entities.text: Subhash Chander v. State, Delhi Administration [1983(4) DRJ 100]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The Director is a greater expert and therefore the statute says that his certificate shall be accepted by the court as conclusive evidence.
For all purposes the report of the public analyst is replaced by the certificate of the Director....
Superseded is a strong word.
It means obliterate, set aside, annul, replace, make void, inefficacious or useless, repeal.
The Director's certificate supersedes the report given by the public analyst.
Once superseded it does not survive for any purpose.
It will be anomalous to hold that for some purpose it survives and for other purposes it is superseded."
15. Since the report of CFL is final and conclusive and the same supersedes the report of PA, only this report has to be considered and the report of PA has to be ignored.

However, the defence strongly relies upon the judgement titled as Kanshi Nath v. State [2005(2) FAC 219], informing that the said ruling has been constantly followed by the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in State v. Ramesh Chand [2010 (2) JCC 1250], Food Inspector v. Parvinder Malik [2014(2) FAC 306], State v. Vinod Kumar Gupta [2010(2) JCC 957], State v. Virender Kohli [2014(2) FAC 223], State v. Kamal Aggarwal [2014(2) FAC 183], State v. Vidya Gupta [2014(1) FAC 291], State v. Dinesh Goswami [2014(1) FAC 302], State v. Mahabir [2014(1) FAC 286], State v. Santosh Sharma [2014(1) FAC 296], Raja Ram Seth & Sons v. Delhi Administration [2012(2) FAC 523], State v. Sunil Dutt [2011(4)
JCC 2377] and State v. Rama Rattan Malhotra [2012(2) FAC 398].

16. sentences.text:
Hon'ble Court considered the ratio in MCD v. Bishan Sarup [ILR 1970 (1) Delhi 518] and held that it would still be open for the accused to establish that the sample tested was not a representative one, and if the variation in the two reports is substantial enough, then the PA report can certainly be looked into to establish this variation.
17.
Therefore, it can be safely said that though the CFL report is final and conclusive as to the results therein, yet it can still be looked into to ascertain if the samples were representative or not.

If the accused is able to show that the samples were not representative or there is possibility that they were not of the same lot or batch, he would get benefit on that count.
18.
Well, the differences between the two reports would show substantive variations in the two reports.

The PA detected saponification and iodine values to be exceeding the prescribed maximum limits of 177 and 112 respectively, but no such violation was noticed by CFL which found these values to be well within the prescribed range.

Not only this, even on the labeling standards, it is noticed that the PA found violation of Rule 32(c) (though it observed that the label was without declaration or batch number, for which Rule 32(e) was applicable).
But no such violation was found by the CFL which termed the sample as misbranded on entirely new ground of Section 2(ix)(g), which was never the case when the sample was analyzed by the PA.
It is therefore seen that the CFL report negated the report of PA on all the parameters on which the sample was failed, both for adulteration as well as misbranding.
It can be said that the sample with the CFL was conforming to the standards as to the nature, quality and substance of the food article.
Since the CFL report supersedes the PA report, it has to be held that there was no deficiency in the food article.
The only question now to be considered is if the sample was misbranded or not.
19. Before going into the CFL report, it is important to note the mechanical manner in which the complaint was filed by the complainant.
The PA opined that the sample was misbranded being in violation of Rule 32(c).
Rule 32(c) pertains to the requirement that every food article should mention complete name and address of the manufacturer.
Apparently, complete details of manufacturer were there on the label of the food article in question.
This is clear even from Form VI on which the contents of the label had been reproduced by the FI.
It is not understood as to on what basis the PA claimed that there was violation of Rule 32(c).
And for that matter, even the FI never bothered to examine or to seek clarification from the PA in this regard.
Even the complaint filed in the court mechanically mentions that Rule 32(c) had been violated.
There is no violation of such rule.
It is noticed that as per PA report, there was no batch number on the label.
For that, the applicable rule was Rule 32(e) but no such violation was alleged even by the complainant.
20. Be that as it may, it is strange to note that no such violation of Rule 32 was opined by the CFL.
There is no such violation reported and thefore, and the court has to take a view that there was no such violation in the sample sent to the CFL.

It is also accepted by the PWs that the words "TF-8"
were mentioned on the label.
Keeping in view the definition of batch number / lot number / code number as given in Rule 32(e), there is nothing to show that the said words cannot be treated as batch number.
This is particularly when no such violation was observed by the CFL.

sentences.text: The ground on which the CFL opined the sample to be misbranded was alleged misleading statement to the effect that the food article was pure, guaranteed and certified unadulterated.

Again,
no such observation was given by the PA and it appears that the PA did not find any such statement misleading or deceptive.
It is again a matter of record that there was "Agmark" on the product.
It is nowhere the case of the prosecution that the food article was not conforming to the standards required to obtain Agmark or that it was not competent to use Agmark on the label.
By its very presence, an Agmark product guarantees the basic minimum guarantee and it can, in common language, be called as a certification as to purity and quality of a product.

Therefore, if the manufacturer claimed his product to be pure and unadulterated, and also certified to be so on the basis of authorized use of Agmark, then there may not be any misleading or deceptive statement.
This is particularly when the CFL found the food article to be otherwise conforming to the standards as to its nature, substance and quality.
22. Therefore, considering the variation in the two reports, not only the point of adulteration but also on the point of misbranding, the accused persons are entitled to be given benefit of doubt.

The evidence on record is not sufficient to conclude that the sample in question was 'misbranded' within the meaning of section 2(ix) of PFA Act and thus, no case would be made out against the accused persons for commission of offences punishable under section 7/16 of the PFA Act.
23.
Having said so, both the accused no.1 and 3 are acquitted of the charges.

However, the bail bond of accused no.1 shall remain in force for the next six months in terms of section 437-A. CrPC.
24.
File be consigned to record room.
The same shall revive upon appearance / apprehension of accused no.4, who continues to be Proclaimed Offender.

Announced in the open court this 19th day of December 2016 ASHU GARG ACMM-II (New Delhi),
